items.title: Nigeria woos Russian investors, seeks local currency trade settlement at Moscow summit
items.description: ‎By Boluwaji Obahopo ‎ ‎Nigeria has called for a shift in its relations with Russia from political commitments to practical economic cooperation, urging Russian investors to explore opportunities in the country’s energy, solid minerals, agriculture, manufacturing, pharmaceuticals and digital sectors. ‎ ‎The Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Sola Enikanolaiye, made the call while delivering Nigeria’s statement at the Third Russia-Africa Summit at the Grand Kremlin Palace, where he also advocated stronger trade and financial arrangements, including independent local currency settlement mechanisms between both countries. ‎ ‎Enikanolaiye, who led Nigeria’s delegation to the summit, said the future of Africa- Russia relations must be measured by tangible economic outcomes, stressing the need to translate longstanding diplomatic ties into investments, technology transfer and development partnerships. ‎ ‎He said Nigeria was particularly interested in strengthening cross-border payment arrangements with Russia through mutually agreed systems, alongside improved banking channels and financial infrastructure to facilitate trade and investment. ‎ ‎The minister, who conveyed President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s greetings to Russian President Vladimir Putin and the African Union Chairman, President Evariste Ndayishimiye of Burundi, said the private sector must play a greater role in driving the partnership. ‎ ‎He urged Russia to collaborate with African countries on commercially viable infrastructure projects covering railways, ports, energy, telecommunications, transport and logistics, noting that such investments would strengthen regional connectivity and support the objectives of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). ‎ ‎On the digital economy, Enikanolaiye warned against Africa becoming merely a consumer of imported technology, calling for expanded cooperation in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, software development, digital infrastructure and joint research. ‎ ‎He said such partnerships should prioritise technology transfer, capacity building and the development of indigenous technological capabilities across the continent. ‎ ‎The minister also identified agriculture and food security as critical areas for cooperation, urging Russia to support African countries in expanding domestic food production, fertiliser availability, irrigation, mechanisation, agricultural research, storage and agro-processing. ‎ ‎According to him, recent disruptions to global supply chains have exposed the vulnerability of food systems, making it imperative for African countries to strengthen domestic production and retain more value from their agricultural resources. ‎ ‎On security, Enikanolaiye reaffirmed Nigeria’s commitment to peace and stability in Africa, identifying terrorism, violent extremism, transnational organised crime, arms trafficking, piracy and cybercrime as threats requiring coordinated regional and international responses. ‎ ‎He, however, stressed that such partnerships must be anchored on African ownership and African-led solutions, with external cooperation strengthening existing regional mechanisms, including the African Union and ECOWAS. ‎ ‎The minister further reiterated Nigeria’s commitment to sovereign equality, territorial integrity, non-interference and the peaceful settlement of disputes, while calling for reforms of the United Nations Security Council and international financial architecture to guarantee Africa’s rightful representation. ‎ ‎On the outcome of the summit, Enikanolaiye said Nigeria supported the adoption of a focused Africa-Russia Action Plan for 2027–2029, with clear priorities, financing arrangements and monitoring mechanisms to ensure that agreements translated into measurable results. ‎ ‎He specifically invited Russian businesses to take advantage of Nigeria’s position as Africa’s largest market and a strategic gateway to West Africa and the AfCFTA, highlighting opportunities in energy, including renewable and nuclear technology, solid minerals, agriculture, manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, defence and digital services. ‎ ‎The minister also said the summit had reinforced the longstanding friendly relations between Nigeria and Russia, recalling Moscow’s historic support for Nigeria’s unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity dating back to the Soviet era. ‎ ‎Speaking at the plenary session, Putin described Russia and Africa as natural allies in building a just multipolar world order, reaffirming his country’s commitment to sovereign equality, expanded diplomatic engagement, security cooperation and greater African representation in global institutions. ‎ ‎Similarly, Ndayishimiye stressed that Africa would not exchange one form of subordination for another, insisting that the continent’s international partnerships must respect its independence and development priorities. ‎ ‎He said the 2027–2029 Action Plan would provide an opportunity to address infrastructure deficits through technology transfer and skills development, while moving Africa from dependence on external assistance towards greater economic independence. ‎ ‎The AU chairman also identified water security as a major priority of the continental body’s 2026 agenda. ‎ ‎These was contained in a statement on Sunday by the Minister’s Special Assistant on Media and Public Communication, Mr. Richard Elesho The post Nigeria woos Russian investors, seeks local currency trade settlement at Moscow summit appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Présidentielle française 2027: Christine Lagarde candidate ?
items.description: L’ex-ministre de l’Economie française, Christine Lagarde sera-t-elle candidate à la présidentielle 2027 pour la succession au président Emmanuel Macron ? Rien n’est moins sûr car la redoutable adversaire de Marine Le Pen a annoncé sa démission à la tête de la Banque centrale européenne pour début 2027, selon des médias, ce dimanche 1 er novembre 2026. La patronne de la Banque centrale européenne (BCE), Christine Lagarde, vient d'annoncer sa démission à la tête de l'institution. L’ex-ministre en charge de l’Economie sous le règne de Nicolas Sarkozy, quittera Francfort au début février 2027, pour s'opposer à Marine Le Pen dans la course présidentielle, selon certaines sources médiatiques. Ancienne avocate d'un grand cabinet américain, Christine Lagarde, à en croire certains analystes politiques, a le profil pour candidater pour l’élection le 2 mai 2027. Pour ces derniers, un élément qui milite en sa faveur est l'absence de candidat capable de dégager un consensus au centre, et de se qualifier pour le second tour face à Marine Le Pen, coiffant ainsi sur le poteau Jean-Luc Mélenchon, le leader de la gauche radicale. items.title: Sahara occidental : le Maroc prend le risque d’une reprise de la guerre
items.description: Le Maroc entend tirer parti de la non-reconduction de la MINURSO pour imposer de nouveaux paramètres au dossier du Sahara occidental . Rabat saisit ainsi une décision du Conseil de sécurité pour tenter de remodeler un processus politique dont il conteste désormais les mécanismes et les contraintes. Maroc : une stratégie à haut risque Cette démarche repose sur un calcul très risqué. En cherchant à réduire l’espace diplomatique et à placer le Polisario devant un cadre exclusif de négociation défini par le Maroc , les autorités marocaines négligent les conséquences de cette stratégie. Elles vont renforcer, au sein du mouvement sahraoui, ceux qui considèrent que la lutte armée demeure le seul moyen d’arracher les droits du peuple sahraoui, après des décennies d’impasse diplomatique. L’intervention de Nasser Bourita sur 2M, le 31 octobre, confirme cette orientation. Le ministre marocain des Affaires étrangères a présenté le veto russe comme une occasion de sortir du cycle annuel de la MINURSO. Il a réaffirmé que l’autonomie sous souveraineté marocaine doit constituer désormais le seul cadre des négociations. Il a également exprimé la volonté de Rabat de redéfinir les modalités de l’action onusienne ainsi que le rôle de l’envoyé personnel du Secrétaire général. Excusez du peu ! Il entend désormais déplacer la bataille diplomatique vers l’Assemblée générale des Nations unies, pour transformer les soutiens bilatéraux en appuis multilatéraux. Rabat cherche à obtenir la capitulation du Polisario En définitive, Rabat cherche à obtenir la capitulation politique du Front Polisario et de la communauté internationale, en les sommant de se plier aux règles du jeu qu’il entend désormais édicter unilatéralement, comme s’il était seul maître des horloges et du processus politique. En agissant ainsi, Rabat joue avec le feu. En cherchant à imposer unilatéralement ses propres règles et à acculer le Front Polisario, le Maroc risque de provoquer une réaction dont il ne mesure pas la portée. Le verrouillage de la voie diplomatique ouvre immanquablement la voie de la reprise de la guerre qui risque de s’imposer comme une option incontournable, si aucune garantie internationale robuste ne prend le relais. items.title: Pakistan’s past and future make a bid for the present
items.description: Whatever there is to be said about Fakhar Zaman has been said. And he has usually said it himself – first when he made his debut and steered Pakistan to their greatest triumph of the past decade, then countless times for Lahore Qalandars, then on that one rainy day in Bangalore, climbing a mountain no one had given him a shot at. Fakhar has had a long few years, with recurring injuries and patches of very lean form, but his penchant of showing up when it matters, in extremely emphatic fashion, hasn’t wavered with time. In a side that gets frequently noted for crumbling under pressure, faltering in the biggest moments, never being quite able to get over the line for true glory, Fakhar has churned out a reputation for himself that is the opposite. A ‘big match player’ is the sort of cliche that seems overwrought, but Fakhar has made it entirely his own. When it matters most, it is foolish to count him out. “The way my last 4 games had gone, a good performance was due,” he said during the post-match ceremony after scoring a match-winning century to lead Pakistan to triumph in the One-day International tri-series final against Sri Lanka on Saturday. Fakhar Zaman celebrates his half century with Saad Baig alongside, during the tri-nation series final at the Gaddafi Stadium, Lahore, on Saturday, 31st October 2026.–AFP “Cricket is just like this, sometimes you are a good knick and sometimes you don’t score; even today I was struggling in the beginning.” “But I know that when it is my day, and the ball is coming onto my bat, I will score big.” And that he did – despite his lean returns in the first four matches Pakistan played in this tri-series, and despite the several scares he survived yesterday - wobbly shots, being dropped and given reprieves, Fakhar showed why giving him a life in a final has been, historically, a bad idea. Pakistan does not have a lot of time left with Fakhar. He is 36 years old, and will be 37 by the time next year’s World Cup in southern Africa is underway. It would probably be the most opportune moment for him to sign off on a memorable career, trying to give his team one shot at the ultimate glory in his favourite format. His century yesterday - 12th in ODIs, a record-breaking fourth in chases of more than 300 - is just one of those things Pakistan fans should learn to cherish when they get. But if yesterday showed anything, apart from reaffirming what Fakhar means to a Pakistan side, it was that Pakistan don’t have to be starved of time. In a match where Pakistan’s most trustworthy southpaw wielded his bat once again, it was one other that let him, and yet another that ensured it wouldn’t go to waste. Saad Baig had big shoes to fill coming into this ODI tri-nation series. With Mohammad Rizwan’s absence, Pakistan was not only missing a cog of the batting line-up that has been so crucial for so long, but also one of the finest pair of wicket-keeping gloves the country has sported. No one else has seemed good enough in comparison behind the stumps - either too undercooked, or too sloppy. Saad was Pakistan’s U-19 captain, and made his debut earlier in this tri-series. With a promising performance behind the stumps, and a string of starts with the bat that left one feeling unfulfilled but entirely assured of the pristine talent that shone through, the 19-year-old came out looking like he had a lot to prove. Ironically, he turns 20 today, following a knock yesterday that can only be described as a coming-of-age. If Fakhar was Pakistan’s anti-thesis to not showing up when it matters, Saad was the anti-thesis to a star performing batter never having enough support on the other end. “I have played domestic cricket with Saad, he is a very talented player,” Fakhar said, adding that Saad briskly scoring runs when he came to the crease yesterday allowed Fakhar to settle and take his time, and ultimately go big. “The credit goes to him for starting the way he did.” “Obviously there is pressure on you whenever you move to international cricket,” said Saad in a video reflection posted on PCB’s social media handles. “But the way you have to play through the pressure and back yourself, I was lacking that in the first two or three games, and was getting out in the 30s,” he added, saying that his plan for yesterday’s innings was to score while staying settled at the crease, and Fakhar’s “outstanding” innings made doing that all the more easier. He rotated strike and got into a good groove with Fakhar, rotating strike and picking out the Sri Lankan bowlers whenever the opportunity came to him. Perhaps the way he got out - an anticlimactic chip back to the bowler on a full Theekshana delivery - reflects where he stands in his career compared to the man across the other end, lacking just the final bit of grit and presence that can only come with time. And if these two left-handers set Pakistan on for victory, another one entirely made sure he finished it. Between overs 32.5 and 42.5, Pakistan did not score a single boundary. Fakhar and Salman Ali Agha had been bowled in quick succession. With Hasan Nawaz and Arafat new on the crease, and most of the toe-end of the innings left to bat through, their game plan seemed simple enough: don’t throw it away. The scoring during those overs came entirely from rotating strike, which might have felt grinding and underwhelming for an audience who had just witnessed a Fakhar Zaman special. Arafat Minhas plays a shot during the tri-nation series final at the Gaddafi Stadium, Lahore, on Saturday, 31st October 2026.–AFP It was a full Asitha Fernando delivery in the 45th over, drilled disdainfully down the ground, that would open the floodgates. In the bowler’s next over, Arafat hit possibly the cleanest, most sublime sequence of shots he has procured in his short career so far, bludgeoning two sixes and a four before holing out with Pakistan just two short of the win. “When I went in [to bat], I told Hasan that we have been through this situation before, and so we tried building a partnership,” he said. The two had carried out a deftly executed rescue job in their first tri-series fixture against England as well, ensuring Pakistan posted a total north of 300. “We backed each other and waited for bad balls to come to us.” “And I think through communicating with each other we had developed confidence in one another as well,” he said. Arafat was awarded player of the series as well - the second time he’s been awarded the title in as many ODI series he has participated in. “I have been saying from the beginning that I am an all-rounder,” he said in the ceremony. He was, after all, the leading architect with both bat and ball in Pakistan’s first win against England. “There is pressure, but the way you enjoy the pressure, stay calm during it, and execute your skills is important,” he said of the tricky place the team found itself in when he came in to bat with Hasan. Pakistan’s ODI assignments now all build up to the big shot at the big prize, the World Cup in South Africa next year. Young talents like Saad and Arafat is blooding in, and stalwarts like Fakhar hoping to find one final burst for the nation. What Pakistan can hope to take to South Africa is a team that sports both, the best of its recent past, and the most promising of its hopefully long future. And three left-handers on Saturday night in Lahore, showed exactly how to do it.

items.title: Forces armées nationales : Plus de 86 000 inscrits à la réserve militaire en moins d’un mois
items.description: Les Forces armées nationales (FAN) ont célébré leur 66e anniversaire ce dimanche 1er novembre 2026, à Ouagadougou, sous le thème « Forces Armées Nationales et Réserve militaire pour une défense souveraine de la Patrie ». Présidée par le président de l’Assemblée législative du peuple, Ousmane Bougouma, représentant le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, la cérémonie a été marquée par un appel à la mobilisation citoyenne et la présentation des enjeux de la réserve militaire. Selon le ministre de la Guerre et de la Défense patriotique, le Général de Division Célestin Simporé, plus de 86 000 personnes se sont déjà inscrites en moins d’un mois, pour un objectif de 100 000 réservistes d’ici à la fin de l’année 2026. La réserve militaire constitue désormais un axe majeur du dispositif national de défense. Dans son discours, le Général de division Célestin Simporé a souligné qu’elle traduit la volonté de préparer les citoyens à contribuer à la protection du territoire, au-delà des seules forces actives. « En adoptant la loi portant statut de la réserve militaire, le Burkina Faso s’est doté d’un instrument stratégique de mobilisation des compétences, de consolidation de la résilience nationale et de renforcement de notre capacité collective à faire face aux menaces » , a déclaré le ministre. Adoptée le 26 mai 2026, la loi n°019-2026/ALP définit la réserve militaire comme une composante des Forces armées nationales constituée de citoyens burkinabè aptes à être mobilisés, sans être des personnels d’active. Elle est destinée à renforcer la défense intérieure et extérieure du territoire national. Pour le ministre, ce dispositif doit fournir aux FAN une force complémentaire rapidement mobilisable en fonction des besoins. Il a toutefois précisé que l’objectif n’est pas de transformer chaque citoyen en soldat, mais de permettre à ceux qui le souhaitent et remplissent les conditions requises de servir dans un cadre légal, organisé et discipliné. Un objectif de 100 000 réservistes en 2026 Le lancement des inscriptions à la réserve militaire suscite un intérêt important au sein de la population. « Avec en moins d’un mois plus de 86 000 inscrits pour un objectif de 100 000 réservistes d’ici la fin de l’année 2026 » , a-t-il indiqué, saluant cet engagement citoyen. Le ministre a lancé un appel à la participation de toutes les catégories de la population, en fonction des aptitudes et des compétences de chacun. « Servir la patrie ne signifie pas nécessairement porter les armes en permanence, mais être prêt à apporter sa contribution lorsque les circonstances l’exigent » , a-t-il affirmé. La réserve militaire comprend deux composantes. La réserve de premier ordre regroupe notamment les anciens militaires des FAN, les anciens personnels des forces de sécurité intérieure, les anciens Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP) et d’autres personnes disposant d’une formation ou d’une expérience militaire reconnue. La réserve de second ordre concerne notamment les anciens appelés ayant bénéficié d’une formation civique et militaire, ainsi que les citoyens volontaires sans expérience militaire préalable. Le recrutement peut se faire par sélection parmi les personnes répondant aux critères de ces composantes ou par appel à candidatures pour les citoyens burkinabè volontaires âgés d’au moins 18 ans. Le service de réserviste est compatible avec l’exercice d’un emploi civil. La souveraineté au cœur de la défense nationale Le thème retenu pour ce 66e anniversaire met l’accent sur la contribution de la réserve militaire à la souveraineté nationale. Le Général de division Célestin Simporé a estimé que cette souveraineté suppose que le Burkina Faso puisse concevoir ses propres réponses aux défis sécuritaires, conduire ses opérations et défendre ses intérêts vitaux. Cette ambition, a-t-il poursuivi, exige des hommes et des femmes bien formés, moralement solides, techniquement compétents et animés par le sens du devoir. La réserve militaire doit également servir de trait d’union entre les Forces armées nationales et la société, en rapprochant l’engagement citoyen des exigences de la défense nationale. Selon les dispositions présentées, les réservistes peuvent être mobilisés en cas de menace à la sécurité nationale, de crise sécuritaire, de conflit armé, de catastrophe naturelle ou de besoin de renforcement des capacités administratives et opérationnelles des FAN. Les réservistes de premier ordre peuvent notamment renforcer les unités opérationnelles, assurer l’encadrement et la formation ou apporter un appui au commandement. Ceux du second ordre peuvent contribuer au renforcement des capacités et aux fonctions de soutien ou de spécialité. Un hommage aux militaires engagés sur le terrain-©Faso7 Le ministre de la Guerre et de la Défense patriotique a également salué les militaires et les Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie engagés sur les différents théâtres d’opérations. Il a rendu hommage à ceux qui poursuivent leur mission loin de leurs familles et dont l’engagement, selon lui, témoigne de la détermination du peuple burkinabè. S’adressant au Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, Président du Faso et Chef suprême des Forces armées nationales, le Général de division Célestin Simporé a exprimé la fierté et la loyauté des personnels militaires, tout en saluant son engagement en faveur de la défense et de la souveraineté du pays. Créées par la loi n°74-60/AN du 3 août 1960, les Forces armées nationales ont connu plusieurs évolutions dans leur organisation et leurs missions. Le transfert officiel du commandement militaire aux autorités voltaïques est intervenu le 1er novembre 1961, date à laquelle est célébré leur anniversaire. Avec la mise en place de la réserve militaire, les autorités entendent élargir les capacités de mobilisation du pays face aux menaces et aux situations exceptionnelles. Josué TIENDREBEOGO Faso7 L’article Forces armées nationales : Plus de 86 000 inscrits à la réserve militaire en moins d’un mois est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Betta Edu courts 500 C’River women, sets 1.5m vote target for Tinubu
items.description: Former Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, Dr Betta Edu, has set a target of 1.5 million votes from Cross River for President Bola Tinubu, come 2027 general elections. Edu, Co-Chairman of the All Progressives Congress (APC) Women Mobilisation Directorate, made the declaration on Sunday in Calabar, during an empowerment programme that benefited about 500 market women, petty traders and artisans. She said the initiative organised at the instance of the First Lady, Oluremi Tinubu, was designed to improve women’s economic livelihood, and strengthen grassroots mobilisation. She said the beneficiaries received N50,000 each, alongside business and household equipment, including deep freezers, blenders, and toasters. According to her, the intervention targets petty traders whose businesses are constrained by inadequate capital. “Some of them are selling trays that have just N5,000 worth of things on them, while some of them have trays with just N10,000 worth of items on them. “So we are giving these sets of petty traders N50,000 each so that they can expand that their business, build on it, so things can get better for them and their children,” she said. Edu urged residents of the state to support Tinubu, Gov. Bassey Otu and other APC candidates as the party was banking on grassroots women’s mobilisation to strengthen its electoral fortunes in the state. She expressed confidence that the state would deliver more than 1.5 million votes for the ruling party, adding that the directorate was establishing support structures for women across the country. She disclosed that the empowerment programme would be extended to other parts of Cross River, with Abi Local Government Area scheduled to benefit in November or December, while the northern senatorial district would be reached in January. The former minister also highlighted some Federal Government interventions, including the student loan scheme and free maternal healthcare, as measures aimed at improving the welfare of Nigerians. As part of the mobilisation activities, she led members of the directorate on a visit to the General Hospital, Calabar, where they interacted with patients, pregnant women and children receiving treatment and offered financial and emotional support. She said the hospital outreach was undertaken at the instance of the First Lady ahead of the APC rally scheduled to hold in Calabar on Monday. Edu also cited subsidised dialysis services and free maternal healthcare as interventions aimed at improving healthcare access and reducing maternal mortality. One of the beneficiaries, Esther Bassey, a widow from Odukpani Local Government Area, expressed appreciation for the support, saying previous empowerment programmes had helped her cater for her three children. Bassey pledged her support for the APC in 2027, saying she and her family would vote for the party The post Betta Edu courts 500 C’River women, sets 1.5m vote target for Tinubu appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: ‎2027: Promote peace, policies, not personal attacks – PDP tells supporters
items.description: By Muhammad Inuwa Dutse ‎ ‎The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Jigawa State has urged its social media supporters to promote peaceful political engagement, issue-based campaigns and policy discussions rather than engage in insults and personal attacks ahead of the 2027 general elections. ‎ ‎The party’s governorship candidate, Mustapha Sule Lamido, made the call during a meeting with PDP social media users and political commentators in the state. ‎ ‎Lamido urged the supporters to use their platforms responsibly by promoting the party’s programmes, policies and candidates through constructive engagement. ‎ ‎He stressed that political campaigns should be driven by ideas and policies capable of winning public confidence, rather than abusive language and personal attacks. ‎ ‎”Political campaigns should focus on issues, policies and programmes that can convince the electorate, not insults or attacks on individuals,” Lamido said. ‎ ‎According to him, the meeting was organised to sensitise youths on the importance of responsible political communication and their role in promoting the party ahead of the 2027 elections. ‎ ‎He further disclosed that the party had completed arrangements to commence its campaign activities across Jigawa State. ‎ ‎Lamido reaffirmed the PDP’s commitment to conducting peaceful and orderly campaign tours across the state, without violence or unnecessary provocation. ‎ ‎”We are committed to peaceful campaigns across Jigawa State, and we urge our supporters to avoid anything that could create tension or disrupt public peace,” he said. ‎ ‎The governorship candidate also expressed appreciation to the people of Jigawa State for their continued support for the PDP, urging them to sustain their confidence in the party. items.title: US hears Pakistan’s concerns over terrorism from Afghanistan, would play ‘productive role’ if there is one: Rubio
items.description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Saturday said that Washington has “heard” Pakistan’s concerns about terrorism emanating from Afghanistan and if “there’s a productive role for us to play, we would play it”. Rubio’s statement came in response to a question about tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan at a press talks in Atlanta. “Pakistan is concerned about terrorist attacks that are being sponsored from the territory of Afghanistan. They feel as if the Taliban have not done enough to constrain those attacks, and they have taken action against it. “We obviously have heard those concerns on their part. We obviously don’t want them to be targeted for terrorism. So if there’s a productive role for us to play, we would play it,” Rubio said. Mentioning that the US did not “necessarily [have] the closest relationship” with the Afghan Taliban, Rubio added: “We’ve heard the concerns that Pakistan has raised and we’ve seen some of those attacks that they point to. We’re against terrorism no matter where it emanates from and who it targets.” Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), that it says are used for attacks in Pakistan. For their part, the Afghan Taliban have avoided taking a categorical position on the TTP and other groups, while rejecting Islamabad’s allegations that Afghanistan is being used as a base for attacks against Pakistan. On Saturday, Pakistan’s information ministry rebuked the Afghan Taliban’s stance on the ongoing conflict between the two countries, assailing its “persistent refusal to address terrorism” emanating from Afghanistan’s soil. The statement came in response to remarks made by Afghan Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid, who blamed Islamabad’s “wrong policies” for preventing a resolution to the conflict and insisted Kabul was not the cause of counterterrorism issues. In its response, the information ministry said the Afghan spokesman’s remarks expose the “regime’s deeply misguided approach and unwillingness to confront the root cause of deteriorating relations with Pakistan”. “The Taliban leadership continues to blame Islamabad’s policies while conveniently ignoring the single most important issue poisoning bilateral relations: its persistent failure to address terrorism emanating from Afghan soil,” it added. Islamabad reiterated that the “Taliban regime’s persistent refusal to address terrorism remains the principal obstacle to normal relations”. Multiple rounds of talks between the two sides last year, facilitated by Qatar and Turkiye , failed to bring about any workable solution, with the Pakistani government saying the Taliban officials gave no assurances on the key issues. Efforts this year made with China’s involvement also resulted in no breakthrough. Russia, the only country to have formally recognised the Taliban government, has also recently renewed its offer to facilitate a settlement if both sides request its involvement. Moscow’s special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, had last month made this suggestion after the latest round of the Moscow Format consultations on Oct 5 ended without a joint communiqué because of differences between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban delegations over references to terrorist networks operating from Afghanistan. When asked about it during a weekly media briefing , Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan had said talks with Afghanistan could not be unconditional. He also rejected suggestions that Islamabad was unwilling to engage with its neighbour, saying it would welcome sincere efforts by friendly countries to help resolve the dispute. He further stated: “At present, I am not aware of any separate, formal Russian mediation initiative being under discussion.” Meanwhile, intermittent skirmishes at the border continue. September witnessed yet another bout of conflict between the two neighbours, with Pakistan carrying out calibrated airstrikes in the border region in response to terrorist attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Those skirmishes continued in October with Pakistani security forces responding to unprovoked fire from the Afghan side along the border in Kurram and Lower South Waziristan’s Angoor Adda , according to security sources.

items.title: Is Radicalism the Answer?
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube As we enter the midterm elections, Americans seem ready to move on from the Trump era, but there remains great disagreement about what should come next and how we might achieve it. The intellectual historian and law professor Samuel Moyn is among those who believe that liberals have become too timid about driving social, political, and economic change. If the Trump era was in part a response to the failures of centrist moderation, as Moyn suggests, then we may need something more radical to get us out of it. David Brooks is one of those centrist moderates, chastened by the many examples when radical change has led to tragic outcomes—including the example of Donald Trump himself. In this week’s episode, David and Moyn discuss emancipation, fallibility, and the disagreement beneath the disagreement. The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: People are fed up. They’re sick of the establishment and the people who’ve been running things. They want change, and they want change now. When people like me are in the middle of this kind of emotional climate, all our alarm bells start going off. We’re all the product of our times, and I grew up in the age of the Cold War. It was an age when all sorts of exhilarating beginnings led to blood-drenched culminations. The lesson I drew from all this is that moving fast and breaking things is not the way to go. I became suspicious of people who wanted to burn everything to the ground and start over. I became, in other words, a moderate—the kind of guy who favors constant but incremental reform. But let’s face it, the moderates of the center right and the center left have not exactly produced heaven on Earth. Instead, problems ranging from climate change, inequality, the federal debt have just festered. So maybe something more radical is needed. That’s why I’m eager to talk to Sam Moyn. Sam teaches at the law school here at Yale, but in his heart, he’s an intellectual historian. He writes and thinks about the ideas behind our politics. Sam and I are both liberals. We’re both members of the intellectual tradition that values democracy, individual freedom, and the free exchange of ideas. We oppose the authoritarianism that seems to be creeping in from both right and left. But Sam and I are different flavors of liberals. I’m the more moderate kind, chastened by the scars of history, cautious about instant radical change, and more inclined to steady reform. I’m curious to know which of us is right about the current moment. Is it me, the incrementalist? Or is it Sam, who’s a little more transformational? That’s why I’m pleased to welcome Sam Moyn to The Permanent Questions . Samuel Moyn: Thanks for having me. Brooks: Oh, it’s a pleasure. I’ve been reminding people that you and I are both liberals. We both share the same broad philosophy, but I think we have different flavors of liberalism, and I want to get into that. I thought I’d spend a few minutes just describing where my world comes from, and then I’m going to ask you where your world comes from. I was a Democratic Socialist in college. I was a revolutionary. I would’ve been with Bernie and Zohran and all those people. And I was assigned a book called Reflections on the Revolution in France by this guy Edmund Burke. And he was like, “The world’s really complicated. You should be careful about what you think you can change, and therefore move incrementally—gradually, slowly, constantly, but incrementally.” I hated that book, and I wrote up a whole bunch of papers of what an idiot this guy Edmund Burke was. So then I go out in the world and I work on the South and West Side of Chicago as a journalist, and two of the places I covered are housing projects called Cabrini-Green and the Robert Taylor Homes. They were designed by planners and University of Chicago sociologists. They tore down the old neighborhoods, they put up these high-rises, and they didn’t bother to talk to the people in the neighborhoods. When they tore down what they thought were rickety old buildings, they tore out the systems of social support the neighbors had built for themselves. By the time I got there, they were hellscapes. Crime, gangs had taken over. They’d made life worse for the people in those neighborhoods. And I’m like, “Holy crap, that guy Edmund Burke, he might’ve been right.” Conservatism in the Burkean sense—or, as I would call it for the sake of our conversation, “moderation”—is basically based on two ideas in my view. One is that social change is really hard, and you could be wrong. Therefore, you should move incrementally so you can adjust. So I go off into my journalism career, and one of the best things I ever covered in my life was the end of the Soviet Union. And I’m there one day in Moscow, and Boris Yeltsin, who was the democratically elected president of Russia, this old Soviet regime, as a last-gasp effort to stay alive, staged a coup. All these tanks rolled into Moscow. And I interviewed a woman in that crowd, a 93-year-old lady named Valentina Kosieva, and I asked her about her life. She’d nearly been executed by the Reds in the civil war after the revolution in 1917. Every bad thing that happened in Soviet history happened to her. And then the final story I’ll tell is I was covering the Middle East about the same time in mid-’90s, and I’m at the home of Shimon Peres, who was prime minister then. And it was a big celebratory dinner with about 50 or 60 people, and I’d say 40 percent of them were Palestinian negotiators on the Oslo Peace Process, 40 percent of them were Israeli negotiators, and the other 20 percent were people like me— pundits and scholars. The atmosphere in that room was so warm because these men, mostly men, had been through years of negotiation, and they thought they had crossed the line, and we were gonna have a two-state solution. We were gonna have peace. It was a time people forget: If you lived in Gaza, you could fly on a Palestinian airline to a Palestinian airport holding a Palestinian passport. We were on our way to nationhood, and Yasser Arafat vetoed the deal. That’s my story. That’s how I came to believe what I believe. Moyn: Well, I’ve just had a much less interesting life than you, it sounds like. I love that we’re starting with thinking about ourselves as different kinds of liberal, because I think a lot of folks who know about both of us would say neither of us is a liberal. You’re a conservative and I’m a leftist. From my youth, I was impressed by liberalism as something that could emancipate people. Starting with myself. I’m from Missouri. My father was an aircraft mechanic, and my mother was a kindergarten teacher, and I went to public schools. I went to university locally, and I read books that basically said, “Modern times is about a new chance for human beings . ” Who’s been in charge? Maybe they were moderates, but mainly patriarchs, priests, presidents, and they told everyone what to do and what not to do. Then something changed, and more people than ever got a chance to come from nothing and go wherever their dreams might take them. Now, I was a child of the ’90s. I’m slightly younger than you, and I went to university in 1990. Of course, that was the end of history, and there were a lot of ideas about how simple it would be to realize universal freedom and equality, not just in this country but on a global scale. We could go back and think about what people got wrong in the ’90s. Because I agree there was a lot. I’m with you that we need a certain amount of caution. I’d call it fallibilism, and everyone ought to be a fallibilist. I might be wrong about stuff. But that can’t mean if we’re liberals, that we give up on emancipation. We keep our eyes on the prize. And then we have a pettier debate about: What’s the right way to get it? I think a lot of people, and you kinda narrated this, were impressed even before the ’90s by a kind of neoconservative view that the state can mess up, and maybe we ought not to be as interventionist as we once thought. The trouble is, and this was something liberals have thought all the way back, that you can also suffer from not enough intervention. Because it’s not as if getting rid of the state leaves everyone free and equal. That’s the kinda libertarian view, not the liberal view. And so I think we’re in a moment when many of us are appreciating something I’ve long believed in since I was a Democratic Socialist, more or less from the beginning, and never changed my mind, which is that sometimes we need to correct the state and keep it at bay, but sometimes we need more of it, ’cause there are other sources of oppression than the state. Brooks: You used that word emancipation . I want to ask you: What do you mean by that? Moyn: I think the great thing about liberalism is that it promised emancipation, and it’s why I’m a liberal. Some people would say it was only the first philosophy of emancipation in modern times, because there was a second that came along, socialism, and you already talked about the dark side of socialism. But actually liberals helped invent socialism, so maybe there was only one framework for emancipation, and it was this liberal one that said we had too much authority and oppression in the past, and we should lift that oppression so that more people in more ways can live the lives they choose. Brooks: As you’re trying to advance the cause of emancipation, how do you think about the epistemological problem? Epistemology is a fancy word for how we know things, basically. James C. Scott wrote a book called Seeing Like a State , which had a huge influence on me. It’s about why a lot of international development projects fail. And he tells a story in there that symbolizes, I think, his whole worldview, which is: There were these German guys who wanted to improve the efficiency of their timber industry. So what they did is they looked at the forest and they said, “Well, there are these nice trees we can use, and there’s all this other crap called underbrush. ”What’s this crap doing here? Let’s clear it out and let’s plant our trees in straight rows so it’ll be efficient.” And it worked for a few years, and then the trees started dying, and because they were German, they invented some new word for forest death . And so Scott’s point of view is that planners, in order to plan for the future, have to simplify reality to make it legible to them. And when they simplify reality, they end up cutting out stuff that’s essential. As you’re doing action, how do you think about that problem? Moyn: I think it’s a balance of risks. I totally accept the view that there can be mistakes that people make. They might not be aware of just how much wisdom there is accumulated over time. And that no planner could reproduce that on the fly, especially if it’s just one person or a small elite. These are views that do come from Burke, and they were revived very famously by neoliberals like Friedrich Hayek. I guess the trouble is that tradition’s a mixed bag, and what we’ve accumulated could be a lot of mistakes. We both love an even older thinker, Aristotle. He said things like “Tradition is often old people repeating the same mistakes.” So we need some winnowing process. I think you’d have to agree with this, especially if we’re fallibilists. We have to say, “Tradition can be wrong.” Once in a while, the planners could sweep away something that needed to be swept away. Surely the fact that old men ruled for all those millennia, men ruled over women, fathers over children, didn’t deserve the deference that you’re suggesting we give it, because it was oppressive. Elon Musk: Is he someone who wields a lot of power over not just the two of us, but millions? Absolutely. Was he ever elected? But that would have to take place by messing with our economy using the state, with all the risks it entails and all the caution that I think you’re right to say we should exercise. The alternative would be doing nothing and leaving the powerful in charge of our lives. Brooks: Let me ask you a question about human nature. Modern biologists insist on it. But as far as I can see, the way societies organize changes what people think and how they act more or less completely. On the other hand, every human I’ve ever met has certain desires for goods. We want to belong. We want love and friendship. We want respect. You look at a kid out on the playground just learning the skateboard—they wanna get better at the skateboard. These, to me, are inborn elements of human nature, and you’ve just got to respect it. And so they said, “We’re just gonna change the political order, but the social order, that’s too deep. The reason I don’t share it is that when we look back at all those centuries and millennia of oppression, the same idea of a fixed human nature was the rationale for the oppression. Why could women—who got the vote not that long ago—why did they have to suffer under patriarchy all of that time? Well, because of the way men are and the way women are and so forth. That was definitely a rationale for chattel slavery, because there were claims about the way white people are and the way Black people are. I come with a kind of default skepticism about such claims because they need to be stress-tested. And what’s significant about modern history—and this would include American history, not just the French Revolution—is that some people stood up and said, “What if we checked how much oppression we absolutely require because of an enduring human nature?” And the answer, on both sides of the Atlantic, was a lot less than people from millennia had thought. Brooks: Just on this human nature question, if you measure the capacities of men and women, of whites and Blacks, you see that the idea that one is mentally or otherwise inferior is just wrong. So that was a stress test. But if you stress-test the idea that human beings all have an urge to dominate, I don’t quote Michel Foucault very often, but he said that we all have a little inner fascist inside, and that’s the one thing with Foucault I agree with. That’s actually proved by rigorous intellectual work. To use error to disprove truth is not a good extension of what we learn from error. Moyn: Fair enough, but we’re in an ongoing experiment. In my way of thinking, for most of the history we know about, oppression was the rule and freedom rare. Then we tweaked a few things. It seems like your view is basically: That was a long time ago and we’re done. And my view would be: We just got started, just a few days ago. When did women even enter the workforce? Do we have a racial income and wealth gap right now, even though we’ve abolished formal apartheid? So even on race and gender, it seems like early days, and then there are a lot of other things like class that we could get into. On the French Revolution, obviously it didn’t go perfectly. I think America lucked out, because it didn’t have the same kind of old regime to overthrow. The revolution took place very far away from pretty much all the other powerful states. Compare the French Revolution, which was much more radical, but part of that was a good thing. It birthed the first ideas that women should be equal. Olympe de Gouges very famously propounded a declaration of the rights of women and citizen. Jews were emancipated from one day to the next. They had an old regime to face down, which had formally assigned people to second-class citizenship, and they thought that had to be swept away. So America had this backwater good fortune to start something. It set up a time bomb that later went off in the 1860s. Many of the ideas in the French Revolution lit the world on fire. Would we have a decolonized world without the French Revolution? Because that was really the model for humanity under empire the world over. So I wouldn’t idolize either the American or French Revolution, but I also think it’s a mistake to say, “The American Revolution was the good one.” What about the slaves? What about the women? Et cetera. Brooks: I have a shallow question. The shallow question is there’s a magazine in America now called The Jacobin . I don’t know if you’ve ever written for The Jacobin . Moyn: I have. It’s like a finger in your eye, like conservatives saying, “Oh, we’re gonna call our magazine the Gestapo .” So that’s my shallow question. Moyn: It gets us into this really disturbing and exciting feature of our time, which is that a lot of people have concluded that the centrist moderates—and you’ve self-ID’d in that direction—that they’ve failed. They killed some people, but the American revolutionaries expelled tens of thousands of loyalists. Some people died in the American Revolution, not just combatants. Almost everyone we met said, “I’m voting for Bernie or Trump. I just can’t decide which.” That’s why I wasn’t shocked that badly later on in that year when Trump won. I mean, I was as blindsided as everyone else. But it was an amazing thing because it showed the appetite out there for new ideas, and if they weren’t gonna come from the left, they were gonna come from the right. The populists in American history have been very hard to locate on the political spectrum. We may need a counter populism of the left in order to finally get what centrists like you say they want, which is finally to contain Donald Trump after decades of betrayal when these working people became so incensed about business as usual. Brooks: We have different diagnoses of how the establishment screwed up and who the establishment is maybe. So a lot of people would look at me, New York Times , The Atlantic , Yale— Moyn: You are the establishment ... Brooks: I am the establishment. I don’t deny that. But I’m disgusted with the establishment. I’m an establishmentarian who’s disgusted by the establishment. I ask myself this question. People like you and I had a better shot, and lots of other people had a better shot. We’ve harvested—if I can use that word crudely—so much more talent in our society. Vietnam, Watergate, the financial crisis, Iraq. I’m not sure any of our institutions are actually working better than they were when the talent pool was like this. Why is that? Brooks: I always say Donald Trump is the wrong answer to the right question. You mentioned the Iraq War indirectly. This was clearly the most serious mistake I made in my intellectual life. I want to tell you why I made it. As I’ve indicated, I was a foreign correspondent in the ’90s. I watched the end of the Soviet Union, and it really was an evil empire. It goes back to Aristotle again, who insists that you need prudence or practical wisdom in order to be an ethical actor, let alone a political one. When we look out at who’s made a big difference politically, they’ve always had this ability, which you’re describing, to judge the situation and exploit opportunities to avoid the biggest risks, and that’s not gonna be asking the Harvard faculty what to do. I mean, that may have been a mistake in Vietnam. But that doesn’t mean we should just ask the first thousand names in the phone book of Cambridge, Mass, either. But I agree with you that certain gifted individuals can make breakthroughs or keep us safe at a scary moment because they have judgment. When he knew well—and I praise him on this point, that folks like John Stuart Mill, who preceded him, thought the point of liberalism was to make our lives creative and interesting. We might need the state to achieve that. And it’s not about equality; it’s about the right kind of freedom. So Berlin’s interesting because part of having this understanding of judgment is also appreciating the self-contradictions that you might be a part of yourself. Brooks: I got out of college, and I worked for a time at National Review with Bill Buckley, and then The Washington Times . I hit all the right-wing spots. Then I was named, at age 25, the book review editor of The Wall Street Journal , which was crazy at that age. But I knew who my heroes were, and they were people around a magazine called Partisan Review . A small magazine, but very influential and very powerful. And by the time I got to them, they were in their 80s. So there was a guy named William Phillips, who was editor of the Review . There was a woman named Diana Trilling, who was the widow of Lionel Trilling. There was a playwright named Lionel Abel. There was a philosopher named Sidney Hook. And there was a historian who I knew the best—I knew Sidney Hook a little—called Gertrude Himmelfarb, who was known as Bea Kristol because she was married to Irving Kristol. And so they were the Cold War liberals, and they were my heroes. You wrote a book criticizing my heroes. Tell us about that argument. Moyn: First off, back when you were a book review editor, neither you nor they were liberals anymore. They had evolved from Cold War liberalism to neoconservatism. Himmelfarb not least, with her husband. I strongly believe that she co-founded the movement with him. That’s why I did a whole chapter on her, really emphasizing how close she was to someone like Reinhold Niebuhr in her youth when she, as a young Jewish woman, championed the civilizational virtues of a kind of very Orthodox Christianity. I think what happened to liberalism is that it was emancipatory. In the middle of the 20th century, the folks that you worshiped kind of abandoned— Brooks: Admired. “Worship” is a little— Moyn: Well, okay. They abandoned liberalism as it had been forged up to that point. That’s because they—very understandably—in the 1940s, after the Weimar Republic had collapsed and the wartime alliance uniting our country with the Soviet Union had come undone and the Cold War had begun, they said the real problem is the left and in particular a left that takes over the state and tramples freedom. That was a very reasonable conclusion at that time. The trouble is, I think that in the shuffle, the reason to be a liberal in the first place got lost. So Berlin redefines freedom, so it’s no longer an emancipatory thing in which the state might have to get involved, but something that is really anti-statist and that’s gonna serve, in the long run, economic liberals—we call them neoliberals—pretty well. Although Berlin hated Hayek, nonetheless, the Cold War liberals like Berlin kind of propound a theory of what freedom is that’s very close to the anti-statist views of someone like Hayek. Not to mention James Scott, who also was influenced by Hayek later on. And then there’s this idea that liberals from the beginning have that it’s not just that the point of life is to be emancipated to make it your own, but that we might have to think about history as something that provides us more and more freedom over time. Because the Soviets made so many claims that they were the vanguard of history, the Cold War liberals said, “No, we should think in the way David Brooks would end up thinking, that we’re basically sinful and there are just strict limits on human possibilities.” But that means that you’re not a liberal anymore because you’re saying there are just limits to what we can ask for, how much emancipation we can hope for. In the end, these folks end up ditching liberalism. I think the results speak for themselves because those Cold War liberals did become neoconservatives, many of them. We don’t know what Lionel Trilling would have done, and his wife Diana famously says he wouldn’t have joined Irving Kristol and Bea Himmelfarb and the rest. But we know what those who lived did. And I believe there’s also a parallel story to tell about how the Cold War liberals accidentally paved the way for neoliberalism. Brooks: I would tell a different story. We’re going to trace the story from FDR to neoliberalism. The neocons, the people I knew, they grew up, a lot of them went to City College, where my grandfather went, and they were all Marxists. They were all communists. And so they’re on the left. Then they grow up and they look at what’s happened to the ideas they believed in. It led to mass murder, on a massive scale. If I would fault your book, it would be you were—you show them reacting, but you don’t show as much what they were reacting to, which was the Gulag. Moyn: Fair enough. Brooks: And so they have that experience. They were all Democrats back in the ’50s. They were all still Democrats. They’re champions of the Great Society. They start a magazine, Irving Kristol does, called The Public Interest , and the first issue of that magazine, they say, “We now understand how to make a government work. We have all the scientific tools. We’ve got the data. It’s all gonna work.” So that’s in the ’60s, and it doesn’t work. You look at the 1970s—inflation’s at 15, unemployment’s at nine, violent crime triples, divorce rates triple, like social chaos. And they think, “We got this wrong too.” And then the third thing that happens: They were poor kids from Brooklyn, and they knew they had made it because their parents were bourgeois and valued hard work, education, and self-discipline. Along come the hippies, who don’t value those things and say, “Bourgeois, those people are boring, empty, soulless.” This generation takes a look at those three things and says, “What the heck? We gotta rethink.” It’s not only them, it’s all of society. All of society takes a look at what I’ve just described, and in 1980 they say: Ronald Reagan. That begins what you call neoliberalism. I don’t believe that’s a thing. I think when you use the word neoliberal , you’re conflating into one neat story Ronald Reagan and Walter Mondale, who were not the same thing. Moyn: Not at all. Brooks: You’re conflating Ronald Reagan and Bill Clinton. And the people who get maddest at the phrase “neoliberal” are the moderate Democrats who say, “We were not part of that party. We were different.” They called themselves New Democrats, and they were more centrist, but they were more centrist precisely because the whole country had shifted to the right. So I don’t like the phrase “neoliberal” for two reasons: It assumes that everybody was Milton Friedman, which was not the case, and it tells a neat story where everything went wrong in that neoliberal era, which we’re now trying to replace. What do you think of the story I just told? Moyn: Well, it’s oversimplified and misleading. Here’s why. The word neoliberal , which used to be marginal, is now very mainstream. Even centrists adopt it to describe what’s happened to our country. It isn’t the view that everyone believed the same thing. The standard view is that there are these orders. There was a New Deal order, and it was so powerful that even though the Democrats founded it, the Republicans were forced to play along. Dwight Eisenhower became a supporter of the welfare state, such as it was. The same argument is then made about the replacement of the New Deal order by the neoliberal order, that what the Reagan Revolution wrought—and absolutely Jimmy Carter started it—then leads Bill Clinton to redefine the goals of the Democratic Party. It’s a fact that some of the old Republicans, like Richard Nixon, were way to the left of Democrats until very recently, until the coming of Bernie Sanders, very precisely. That’s because these anti-statist views—that basically said the state is so prone to mistake that we should abandon it and let private ordering take its place—proved hegemonic across the aisle. Now we’re seeing that you can have too much anti-statism if it paves the way to Donald Trump. And I suspect that on both sides of the partisan spectrum we’re seeing a kind of backlash against the backlash. That’s why you see, not just on the left, people reclaiming the state. You see common good conservatism and all kinds of arguments about the role the government should play in trade and industrial policy—Oren Cass’s ideas about what a conservative economics should look like. So neoliberalism is being broadly abandoned, on both sides of the aisle, because it was hegemonic on both. Brooks: The story you tell that the conservatives were sort of the sun party and the Democrats were the moon party—there’s a lot of truth to that. I mean, Teddy Kennedy sponsored deregulation regulations in the 1970s. So my question is: What was so bad about that era? From the 1980s to, let’s say, 2010—I’m going to conveniently say 2008—we had the greatest reduction in poverty in world history. We had the greatest rise of longevity in world history, the greatest reduction of global inequality in world history. We had growth rates. We had longevity increases. I’m not saying there were not problems in the ’80s and ’90s, most especially with the working class. But it doesn’t strike me as the worst period on Earth. Times change, and problems change, and people move on. I’m for moving on. I’m not going back to where Milton Friedman was. But what was wrong with that period? Moyn: Well, first of all, there’s a lot to what you say. I’m not claiming that there was just an evil time and nothing good happened. A lot of the facts you reported followed from a very particular policy to integrate China into the global economic system, because that’s where you see the anti-poverty succeeding. But basically, I don’t think it’s gonna be credible to say, “There was an era and it felt good and some good things happened, and then everything changed in a new era where we have to rethink.” Because when we rethink, what we learn is that the first era made possible the second era. So then we have to revisit: What did we get wrong, precisely in the ’90s, when I think we both thought a lot of problems had been solved. I think everyone is in the position, having lived through the end of history, of realizing it wasn’t over, and that’s because of mistakes made when we thought it was. Brooks: I was a really enthusiastic Reagan-Thatcher kind of person ’cause I thought our core problem back then was dynamism. We were stagnating. And we needed somebody to increase economic dynamism. They offered, I thought, a plausible thing, and I think they succeeded. Starting in 2003, I look around and think, Our core problem is not dynamism anymore. That’s just a fact. Our core problem is inequality . And so I called up all my old conservative economist friends and said, “Well, what are our conservative ideas on inequality?” They’re like, “I really haven’t done much work on that.” So I would just say the problems have changed. And this is where I’m gonna ask you a question. Inequality’s still obviously a problem. Since I’ve talked in terms of balances, in what way are we out of whack? When historians look back on 2026, what’s the core problem that society needed to address? Moyn: I’m just trying to broaden your diagnosis, and the diagnosis has something to do with elite misrule. In your view, and I share it, there’s a meritocratic elite that doesn’t have the goods, and mainly uses its elite status to lord over ordinary people, and is contemptuous of them, and then is appalled and shocked when they vote for some Neanderthal. I just want to say, it turns out that elite misrule has many facets, and cultural predominance is just one. There’s also economic predominance. More and more people are voting because of their perception of their economic situation. Now, in global history, and especially compared to stagnant European economies, America is often seen to be doing rather well, even right now. But I think people’s everyday experience is that they are living paycheck to paycheck. They are in so-called bullshit jobs that they don’t want, and are underpaid for the work as prices rise, and that’s why this affordability meme has been so successful. It’s not that there’s some obvious fix to that in a global economy. But we can see the way in which the policy choices made way back when by conservatives and liberals led to not just a cultural elite but an economic elite. That’s the story that was, once again, very marginal and is now mainstream of the 1 percent and the increasing economic inequality. Last, you look at foreign policy. Both parties have been warlike and don’t have a lot to show for it. Donald Trump, sadly, was able to claim to be a kind of peace candidate, #EndEndlessWars. That was credible to 70 to 80 million Americans in two big elections. Now, of course, he’s thrown it all away by being just as warlike as those he attacked. Those are three examples of elite failure, and I don’t see how we can just stick with one. Brooks: I can’t help asking you—when I lived in Europe in the early ’90s, America was richer than the European countries, but not by a lot. Now, America’s significantly richer. It’s, like, 30 percent higher. Countries like France, Germany, UK, they’ve got GDP per capita lower than Mississippi. So as a person of the right, or center right, I have a story to tell that they overregulated. What story do you tell to explain that? Moyn: Might be true. They have made an existential choice to have a superior welfare state. Insofar as that involves a much higher taxation, they may have paid a price. On the regulatory front, it’s a big claim you’re making, and it just seems like we’d have to check it out. I’m not saying it’s wrong, but I’m not as confident as you that it’s right. The question is: Can we have regulatory regimes of the kind that Richard Nixon was for—great environmentalist and so forth—that are not impeding growth but actually create new forms of growth, like green energy? If that’s what the Europeans are for, maybe there’s a way of doing it that would have a different outcome. Brooks: I’m gonna promote a grand compromise that I hope can bring us together. I’m about to solve all our polarized problems. Moyn: Wonderful. Brooks: I call it the Sweden Compromise. The Scandinavians figured out a way to have successful societies, and that way is to have a pretty generous welfare state. But it’s also the only way you can afford a generous welfare state if you have free market policies. So people think they’re sort of socialist. They are not. The Heritage Foundation has this index of economic freedom. Heritage Foundation, very right-wing. They measure tax rates, regulation, all that, and Denmark, Sweden, all Scandinavian countries, way above the U.S., way more free market. They have low corporate taxes. They have no wealth tax. They have no minimum wage. Sweden has school vouchers. In Denmark, for example, if you lose your job, you get support for two years, but there are almost no regulations governing when somebody can get fired from a job. So they’ve basically made the decision, lots of free market on the supply side and lots of welfare state on the demand side. I could live with that compromise that the Scandinavian countries have arrived at, maybe with a smaller government than they have. But on the whole, I’d be willing to support a more generous welfare state if you would give me the engines of growth. I say that because I think in the age of AI, we need a lot of job growth. There’s going to be a lot of turnover. Some jobs are going to be destroyed. So we have to create tasks for people to do. You need a lot of economic dynamism. And so that’s my compromise. How does that sound to you? Moyn: I’d potentially take it. But I think we would have to consider whether everything they’ve done is portable to other places. They don’t have the history of race. They do share our newfound immigration restrictionism, which is a way of, in their view in the Nordic countries, of keeping the social basis for solidarity. That just doesn’t seem available to us, and it’s probably a good thing, because I’m sure both of us think that the diversity of the United States, including from immigrant waves, has been, at times, to its benefit and maybe could be again. But that’s just a big difference that might make it very difficult to achieve the compromise even if we agreed with it. But I’m personally for growth, because I think we need to balance dynamism and care. I do think we should have a broader definition of creativity that doesn’t just associate it with economic enterprise and with growth in our wealth. But it’s not as if we can disregard those questions. Where we might differ slightly is I think there’s a genuine question with the rise of AI whether we should keep working, or how big a part of our lives work needs to be or is going to be. John Maynard Keynes, the great economist back in the day, said, “We’re about to solve the economic problem, which will leave us with the big problem, which is how do we spend our lives when we don’t have to provide the means of our subsistence?” AI might be setting up a world in which we finally do face that question. It might make it scarier because not having a lot to do can lead people to make big mistakes. But it’s not as if just planning to replace jobs is the obvious answer to current events. Brooks: On that note of agreement, Sam Moyn, it’s been a real pleasure having a conversation with you. Thank you for coming on The Permanent Questions . Moyn: Thanks for having me. Brooks: All political visions are based on a conception of human nature. What are people like? For Sam, they’re pretty malleable. For me, they’re not so malleable. I think that human beings are beautifully made and deeply broken. We differed on all sorts of things, but it all went down to that original disagreement about the idea of what is a human. And there’s a great Talmudic scholar idea: Find the disagreement under the disagreement. I think that in this conversation, we found the disagreement under the disagreement, and that’s an illuminating thing to do. Thanks so much for joining us for this week’s conversation with Sam Moyn. This podcast is produced by The Atlantic and made possible by support from Yale University. New episodes of The Permanent Questions come out on Sundays. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube page, Apple, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts. If you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. See you next week.

items.title: [Revue de presse] : remaniement judiciaire, nouvelle présidence à la FGF… les principaux sujets à la Une des journaux
items.description: L’actualité guinéenne a été particulièrement riche cette semaine dans les colonnes des hebdomadaires. Le Lynx, La Lance et L’Observateur ont notamment consacré leurs Unes au vaste remaniement intervenu dans les cours et tribunaux du pays, à l’élection du nouveau président de la Fédération guinéenne de football (FGF), ainsi qu’aux mesures prises par le ministre de la Justice pour assurer la continuité du service public judiciaire. Dans sa parution n° 1802 du 26 octobre 2026, l’hebdomadaire satirique Le Lynx a choisi de mettre en lumière les mouvements au sein de l’appareil judiciaire guinéen avec ce titre à sa Une : « Guinée : Mouvement dans les cours et tribunaux du bled. La valse des robins ! » Dans son analyse, le journal revient sur les conséquences des nouvelles nominations et mutations opérées par le président Mamadi Doumbouya à travers un décret du 21 octobre 2026. Notre confrère estime que ces changements interviennent à peine quelques semaines après la rentrée judiciaire 2026-2027, tenue le 5 octobre, et s’interroge sur leurs répercussions sur le fonctionnement des juridictions. Le Lynx dénonce notamment une instabilité persistante au sein du département de la Justice et des Droits de l’Homme, qui a connu cinq ministres en cinq ans sous le régime du CNRD. Le journal évoque une succession de mutations et de nominations qui, selon lui, ne permettrait pas aux magistrats de s’installer durablement dans leurs fonctions. Le périodique souligne également l’ampleur du dernier remaniement, qui a touché plusieurs structures de l’appareil judiciaire, notamment l’Inspection générale des services judiciaires, la Cour suprême, les cours d’appel de Conakry et de Kankan, ainsi que de nombreux tribunaux de première instance. Une nouvelle redistribution des postes qui intervient après les importantes nominations de novembre et décembre derniers. De son côté, La Lance, dans sa parution n° 1550 du 28 octobre 2026, s’est intéressé à l’élection du nouveau président de la Fédération guinéenne de football. Le journal barre sa Une avec ce titre : « Guinée : Présidence de la Fédération guinéenne de football. Un Mamady en cache un autre ! » Dans ses colonnes, l’hebdomadaire revient sur l’élection de Mamady Doumbouya, organisée le mardi 27 octobre, huit mois après la révocation de Bouba Sampil. Le nouveau président de la FGF, directeur général de l’ARPT et président du conseil d’administration de l’Union FC de Conakry, a remporté le scrutin avec 21 voix, devant l’ancien président de l’instance, Mamadou Antonio Souaré, qui en a obtenu 18. Sur les 53 membres statutaires, 52 ont pris part au vote. Ibrahima Khalil Kaba, président du Karfamoriah FC, est arrivé en troisième position avec 13 voix, tandis que Mohamed Chérif Haïdara n’a recueilli aucun suffrage. Le journal revient également sur les circonstances de cette élection particulièrement disputée, marquée notamment par l’absence de prise de parole du candidat Mamady Doumbouya devant les électeurs avant le scrutin. Celui-ci avait laissé cette tâche à l’un de ses proches collaborateurs. Une victoire qui met fin aux ambitions de retour d’Antonio Souaré à la tête de l’instance dirigeante du football guinéen. Dans le même registre, L’Observateur, dans sa parution n° 1324 du 26 octobre 2026, s’est penché sur les mesures prises par le ministre de la Justice et des Droits de l’Homme à la suite du remaniement judiciaire. Le journal titre : « Remaniement judiciaire en Guinée : les directives du Garde des Sceaux après le décret du président Doumbouya ». Notre confrère met en avant les instructions données par Ibrahima Sory II Tounkara pour éviter toute interruption dans le fonctionnement des juridictions à la suite des nombreuses mutations de magistrats. Selon le journal, le Garde des Sceaux a instruit l’ensemble des services concernés d’organiser les cérémonies de passation de service entre le 26 et le 30 octobre 2026 inclus. Ces opérations doivent se dérouler sous la coordination des chefs de cour compétents, en collaboration avec l’Inspection générale des services judiciaires et pénitentiaires. Les magistrats concernés sont notamment tenus d’assurer la remise effective des dossiers, registres, archives, moyens de service et autres documents nécessaires à l’exercice des fonctions transférées. L’Observateur revient également sur les consignes relatives à la gestion des délibérés. Les magistrats appelés à quitter leurs fonctions ne sont pas autorisés à vider les délibérés en instance ni à en prononcer les décisions. En revanche, ceux qui ont déjà rendu des jugements, mais dont la rédaction n’est pas achevée, doivent finaliser les documents et les signer avant leur départ effectif. Enfin, le journal souligne l’obligation d’établir un inventaire contradictoire des procédures en cours, avec une attention particulière accordée aux dossiers impliquant des personnes détenues, aux affaires nécessitant des actes urgents ou exposées à des délais de prescription imminents, ainsi qu’à la vérification et à la transmission des scellés, valeurs et objets placés sous la responsabilité des services concernés. Autant de dispositions destinées à garantir une transition ordonnée et à préserver la continuité du service public de la justice malgré les changements intervenus dans les juridictions du pays. A la semaine prochaine L’article [Revue de presse] : remaniement judiciaire, nouvelle présidence à la FGF… les principaux sujets à la Une des journaux est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.description: CAIRO, Nov 1 (Reuters) - Israeli strikes killed at least eight Palestinians, including five police officers, in the Gaza Strip in two separate attacks on Sunday, according to medics and the Hamas-run interior ministry. Medics said three people were killed in an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City. The interior ministry said the five police officers were killed in another strike in western Khan Younis, in the south of the enclave.

items.title: JOJ Dakar 2026 : l’Équatorienne Elvira Espinosa décroche la première médaille d’or des Jeux
items.description: Les premières médailles des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) Dakar 2026 ont été décernées ce dimanche 1er novembre au Complexe Tour de l’Œuf. L’Équatorienne Elvira Espinosa est entrée dans l’histoire de cette édition en remportant la première médaille d’or de la compétition. Engagée dans l’épreuve du 400 m nage libre, la nageuse équatorienne s’est imposée en 4 min 22 s 87, signant ainsi le premier sacre de ces JOJ Dakar 2026. Une performance qui lui permet d’inscrire son nom au palmarès de cette première édition des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse organisée sur le continent africain. C.G.D
